transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been going on that brought you here today?

I'm here because... well, I just don't care about anything anymore. It's like a switch flipped. I used to go to art classes at the community center, you know? The instructor, Mr. Henderson, he had this weird habit of always wearing suspenders, even when we were doing messy charcoal stuff. He told me I had a good eye for shading. But now... I don't even look at my sketchpads. They're just gathering dust on my desk next to this old lamp I bought at a garage sale. The guy who sold it to me said it was from the 1950s, but honestly, I think it's just a cheap knockoff from Target. Anyway, I don't care about the art, or my board-game nights, or hiking... I used to love hiking up at the state park. The trees smell so good after it rains. But now I just sit in my room. I don't even want to get back on the soccer team. I just sit there while everything slips away.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, it really started to get constant around... I guess it was the summer after I took that geology class. So, about a year and four months now. It's been a long time. But yeah, that geology class, we went on this field trip out to the quarry, and I found this rock—it looked like it had a tiny fossil in it, maybe a fern or something. The professor, Dr. Aris, he was always so enthusiastic about sedimentary layers. He drove this beat-up old Volvo that smelled like wet dog and old coffee. He said it was a reliable car, but it broke down on the way back from the quarry. We had to wait on the side of the highway for two hours for a tow truck. The tow truck driver had this massive beard, like ZZ Top, you know? He kept telling us stories about all the weird things he'd seen on the road. But yeah... it's been about a year and four months of just... feeling like this.
Have you noticed that things you used to enjoy, like art or hiking, no longer give you any pleasure or satisfaction?

Yeah, exactly. Like I was saying before, I just... I don't care about any of it anymore. There's zero satisfaction. Not the art classes, not the board-game nights, not hiking. I don't even care about getting back on the soccer team. I just sit in my room while everything slips away. 

Which is a shame because our soccer team was actually pretty good. We were called the Mud Hens. Our goalie, Sarah, she always brought these thick orange slices for halftime in this huge vintage blue Tupperware container. I wonder if they even still make Tupperware like that? My mom used to have a whole cabinet full of it, mostly that weird avocado green color from the 70s. She used to store everything in them, even spare buttons and sewing thread. Actually, she had this one metal tin that looked like it was for Danish butter cookies, but it was always just sewing supplies. It was such a letdown when you opened it wanting a cookie and just found a bunch of needles and safety pins. But yeah, no... I don't get any joy out of the things I used to do.
Have you felt this way continuously for at least two years, or has there been a time when you felt better for a while before feeling like this again?

Well, it hasn't been two years quite yet, but almost. It started shortly after my divorce, so it's been about a year and eleven months now. My ex-husband, Mark, he took the dog when he left. Buster. He was this goofy golden retriever mix we adopted from the shelter on 5th street. The shelter volunteers were always so nice, especially this older woman named Betty who knitted these little sweaters for the smaller dogs in the winter. She used this really scratchy wool yarn, though, mostly in bright purple and mustard yellow. I tried knitting once, bought all the needles and a bunch of yarn from Michaels, but I could never get the tension right. My stitches were always too tight, and my hands would cramp up. I think I still have the knitting needles somewhere in a box in the hall closet, right next to the vacuum cleaner that keeps making this weird high-pitched whining noise. I should probably get that looked at, or just buy a new one. But yeah, it's been a year and eleven months of feeling this way.
Have you had any period lasting several months when you felt significantly better, where you were able to enjoy things again or feel more like yourself?

No... no, not really. There hasn't been any break. Most of the time since this whole thing took over, I haven't just been, you know, scared of the voices or confused about what's real... I've been deeply, deeply depressed. Just barely interested in anything. I feel like my life is already over. 

Which is a terrifying feeling, honestly. It's like watching a movie where you already know the ending is tragic, but you still have to sit through the whole two hours. I used to love going to the movies, especially the matinees when the theater was practically empty. You could sit right in the middle, prop your feet up on the seat in front of you—even though they tell you not to. The floor always had that sticky feeling, no matter which theater you went to. I think it's spilled soda that they just mop over with dirty water. I read an article once about how much bacteria is actually on movie theater seats, and it was horrifying. They swabbed the armrests and found traces of all sorts of things. But I guess that’s just life, right? Bacteria is everywhere. Even on our phones. I tried cleaning my phone screen with those little alcohol wipes, the ones that come in the tiny square packets. My dad used to keep a handful of those in his glove compartment, right next to the spare fuses and a map of Ohio. He refused to use GPS. Said it was making people lose their sense of direction. But yeah... no, there hasn't been any time where I felt better or felt like myself again. Just this heavy, dark feeling, all the time.
